name: Sorites paradox
statement: Asked about a borderline case, people accept both 'it is tall and not tall' and 'it is neither tall nor not tall', and they accept the second more readily than the first.
meaning: The paradox runs on two premises that each look safe. A hundred thousand grains of wheat make a heap, and if n grains make a heap then so do n minus one. Repeat the second premise and one grain makes a heap. Alxatib and Pelletier give the argument in that form and credit it to Eubulides in the 4th century BCE. Since Wright's paper of 1976 the second premise has been called the tolerance principle: a vague predicate is insensitive to changes small enough. Égré states it generally: if P applies to x, and x and y differ only slightly in the respects relevant to P, then P applies to y. Something has to give, and every position on what gives is a position about vagueness rather than a finding. Epistemicism says there is a sharp boundary nobody can know. Supervaluationism says the predicate is made precise in many admissible ways and is true only where all of them agree, which leaves borderline cases neither true nor false. Subvaluationism takes truth in one admissible sharpening as enough, which leaves borderline cases both true and false. Degree theories assign truth values between 0 and 1. Alxatib and Pelletier set out the first three and Égré lists where each stands on tolerance. The fallacy that borrows the name is a separate object. Égré, Ripley and Verheyen distinguish two argument shapes built on a chain of small steps. The horrible-result form concludes that the first step is bad because the last one is. The arbitrary-result form concludes that there is no step at which it is rational to accept one case and refuse the next. The second is what fallacy lists call the continuum fallacy. It is the shape in the Blackburn passage they quote, where someone says 'there is no principled place to draw a line, so we can't have a limit'. Entry 412 covers the slippery slope, whose causal version claims that one step raises the chance of the next. That is a claim about the world. This one is a claim about a category.

origin.who: Nicolao Bonini, Daniel Osherson, Riccardo Viale and Timothy Williamson
origin.note: The first psychological experiment on the question, not the origin of the puzzle. Its abstract, read at the Oxford University Research Archive, says most speakers experience unclarity about applying predicates like tall and red to liminal cases, and advances a psychologised version of the vagueness-as-ignorance theory. The two accounts fetched here disagree on the ancient credit. Alxatib and Pelletier name Eubulides of Miletus and the 4th century BCE. Égré, Ripley and Verheyen quote Peirce and Baldwin's Dictionary of Philosophy and Psychology of 1902. It separates a marked sense, the sophism of the heap of wheat credited to Eubulides of Megara, from a neutral sense in which a sorites is any chain of syllogisms. Neither Peirce and Baldwin nor any ancient source was obtained here.

evidence: Four things have been measured: where people put the boundary, what they say about cases inside it, what happens when the cases arrive in order, and how categorisation relates to bare discrimination. On the first, Bonini and colleagues asked Italian students for the smallest height that makes it true to say a man is tall, and separately for the greatest height that makes it false. The truth answers came out above the falsity answers, leaving a gap. That design and its numbers are reported here as Alxatib and Pelletier describe them, since the 1999 paper itself was not obtained. There were 652 students in total, 320 asked about truth and 332 about falsity. For tall across four trials, the truth-judgers gave 178.30, 179.55, 181.49 and 170.28 centimetres, the falsity-judgers 167.22, 164.13, 160.48 and 163.40. Alxatib and Pelletier then ran their own study on 76 Simon Fraser University undergraduates, 63.2% of them native English speakers. Each saw a five-man police lineup at 5'4", 5'7", 5'11", 6'2" and 6'6", and marked True, False or Can't tell against four sentences per man. For the 5'11" man, 46.1% called 'he is tall' true and 44.7% called it false, while 25.0% called 'he is not tall' true and 67.1% called it false. People denied a sentence more readily than they asserted its negation, chi-square(2) = 8.22, p < 0.05. Can't tell was rare, 9.2% for 'tall' and 7.9% for 'not tall'. The contradictory sentences peaked at the same man: 44.7% called 'he is tall and not tall' true and 53.9% called 'he is neither tall nor not tall' true. Of those who accepted the neither sentence, 53.7% also accepted the both sentence, and 68.8% of the sixteen people who accepted the both sentence had called each conjunct separately false. Égré and Zehr reproduce the same cross-tabulation from the published version, 34 of 76 accepting the both sentence and 41 accepting the neither one, and report a McNemar-Bowker test of 8.04, p < 0.05. Their review also carries figures from two studies not obtained here. Ripley showed 7 circle-and-square pairs at varying separations and had participants rate sentences from 1 to 7, and on Égré and Zehr's summary of that data no preference between the two sentence types is visible. Serchuk, Hargreaves and Zach used verbal scenarios instead of pictures. They asked readers to imagine a woman somewhere between women who are clearly rich and women who are clearly non-rich. On the table Égré and Zehr build from their data, 'x is P and x is not P' drew 66 true against 195 false. The wordier 'x is P and it is not the case that x is P' drew 25 true against 247 false. Égré, de Gardelle and Ripley took the question to colour. Nineteen French speakers saw 15 shades running between blue and green and between yellow and orange, in random, ascending and descending order, in a perceptual matching task and in a naming task, 1,440 trials each. Order moved the switch point in the naming task, F(2,19) = 24.78, p < 0.001, and not in the matching task, p > 0.3, with the interaction at F(2,19) = 33.09, p < 0.001. The switch came earlier than in random order rather than later, which is negative hysteresis. A second experiment on 26 participants replaced the forced choice with agreement to sentences and recovered the same order effect, F(2,48) = 6.43, p < 0.005 for positive sentences and F(2,48) = 3.40, p < 0.05 for negated ones. It also found the hump. Agreement with 'the square is yellow and orange' and with 'the square is yellow and not yellow' peaked at the middle shades, above agreement with either conjunct there, by 12% on the yellow-orange set and 21% on the green-blue set. The hump reached the conventional threshold in both positive conditions and in three of four negated conditions, failing only for 'yellow and not yellow', t(22) = 1.14, p = 0.27. Égré and Zehr then put 148 Amazon Mechanical Turk workers through verbal scenarios with eight relative gradable adjectives. In mixed-effects logistic models, and-descriptions were accepted more often than control false descriptions, z = 7.60, p = 2.89e-14, less often than neither-descriptions, z = -8.98, and neither-descriptions less often than control true descriptions, z = -3.66, p = 0.000248. Order mattered: acceptance of and-descriptions fell from about 50% to about 35% when the antonym block came first. Where the boundary sits is partly personal. Verheyen, Dewil and Égré recruited 582 Dutch-speaking volunteers, kept 337 after four screening criteria, and had them judge 34 pictograms for tallness and 34 drawings for heaviness. Thresholds correlated with the judge's own measurements: .31 between men's height and the threshold they used on male figures, and .21 to .24 for women on female figures. Women placed the tallness threshold on average 3.48 cm above their own height, standard deviation 6.99, and men 2.10 cm above theirs, standard deviation 6.79. The psychophysical form of tolerance is older. Égré, Ripley and Verheyen trace it to Fechner's just noticeable difference. They quote Luce's 1959 statement that alternatives discriminated more than 100 pi per cent of the time are more than one JND apart, so that it is meaningless to speak of JNDs without specifying the cutoff. Because indifference so defined is not transitive, sequences whose neighbours are within one JND but whose ends are not are easy to build; Luce's example is 401 cups of coffee with increasing sugar. Their reading of the psychophysical literature is that the categorisation premise is not endorsed in its flat form but weakened to a probabilistic one, where near-identical items get near-identical probabilities of being called P rather than the same verdict. Two further results in their review bear on that. Hampton, Estes and Simmons found a contrast effect. Shown a borderline blue-purple patch beside a context patch more than one step away, participants were less likely to give the two the same name. Assimilation appeared only at one step, and the pattern held for cat-to-dog morphs. Stöttinger and colleagues' 40 morphing picture sets of 15 images each produced almost perfect naming at both ends, with third names for the middle pictures peaking around 10% on average.

replication.headline: That people assent to contradictory descriptions of borderline cases has been found by four groups, across pictures and verbal scenarios and in English, French and Italian, and it holds up. What it means is still argued.
replication.detail: It first appeared in 2011 in two independent studies with nothing in common but the question. One was Ripley's circle-and-square ratings. The other was Alxatib and Pelletier's police lineup, where 44.7% of 76 people called the middling man 'tall and not tall' and 53.9% called him 'neither tall nor not tall'. Serchuk, Hargreaves and Zach found the same assent with no pictures at all. Égré, de Gardelle and Ripley recovered it in French on colour continua, where conjunctive descriptions were accepted 12% and 21% more than their own conjuncts at the crossover, on two colour sets. Égré and Zehr's 148 participants, the largest sample in this literature, put both contradictory forms above outright false controls and below outright true ones, and found the gappy form preferred to the glutty one, z = -8.98. That preference was visible in Alxatib and Pelletier's data and invisible in Ripley's, which is the one point on which the studies diverge. The dynamic result has its own replication record. Negative hysteresis means an earlier switch than random order gives rather than a later one. It was reported by Kalmus in 1979, by Raffman with Lindsey and Brown, by Égré, de Gardelle and Ripley in two experiments, and by Stöttinger and colleagues on 40 picture sets. Égré, Ripley and Verheyen call those results consistent with one another. They note that part of the philosophical literature, reasoning from introspection, had predicted the opposite direction. Their own footnote on the Stöttinger data is less comfortable than the headline. More individual series show participants switching later than earlier, and most show no difference in either direction. The largest single effect comes from a series whose endpoint image 34% of participants could not identify. What has not survived is the reading Bonini and colleagues put on their own result. Serchuk, Hargreaves and Zach state in their abstract that they found methodological difficulties in those experiments and devised revised versions that do not show the same results.

study.cite: Égré, P., & Zehr, J. (2018). Are Gaps Preferred to Gluts? A Closer Look at Borderline Contradictions. In E. Castroviejo, L. McNally & G. Weidman Sassoon (Eds.), The Semantics of Gradability, Vagueness, and Scale Structure, pp. 25-58. Springer.

limits: The samples are small and narrow. Alxatib and Pelletier used 76 undergraduates at one campus, Égré, de Gardelle and Ripley 19 and 26 people in one Paris laboratory, and the largest study read here is 148 workers on Mechanical Turk. Égré and Zehr restricted themselves to relative gradable adjectives such as tall, excluding absolute ones such as full, and say the extension to absolute adjectives is open. Their own data shifts with presentation order, from about 50% to about 35% acceptance of the same sentences depending on which block came first, which is a large swing for a finding about semantics. The philosophical solutions are not tested by any of this. Epistemicism, supervaluationism, subvaluationism and degree theories are positions about what vague predicates mean. Every paper read here argues from data to a position rather than testing one against another. Alxatib and Pelletier read the same Bonini data as support for gap theories that Bonini and colleagues read as support for an epistemic account. On the tolerance principle itself, nothing obtained here reports what people say when the inductive premise is put to them as a premise. Serchuk, Hargreaves and Zach's abstract, read at the author's own site and at Crossref, says they compared the persuasiveness of different formulations of it. Their paper could not be obtained. The publisher's copy is paywalled and the open-access copy at PhilPapers returned 403 on repeated attempts, so their four studies are represented here only through the tables Égré and Zehr build from their data. Ripley's 2011 chapter and Bonini and colleagues' 1999 paper were also not obtained, and every figure attributed to them on this page came through a later paper that reproduces it. Égré, Ripley and Verheyen describe Raffman's colour study with Lindsey and Brown as originating in unpublished work. Égré and Zehr name Solt and Gotzner's study on where people leave gaps as unpublished. No figure from either is quoted here. Alxatib and Pelletier's numbers were read in the authors' manuscript hosted on Égré's seminar page rather than in the Mind & Language version, and the cross-tabulation Égré and Zehr take from the published version agrees with it. The psychophysics is reported here as Égré, Ripley and Verheyen present it, including the Fechner, Luce, Hampton and Stöttinger material; those primary sources were not opened.
misreadings: The paradox and the fallacy are not the same object, and this page carries both because the fallacy is named after the paradox. The paradox is a question about what vague predicates mean. The fallacy is an argument that because no line can be drawn without arbitrariness, no distinction holds, which is the arbitrary-result shape Égré, Ripley and Verheyen separate from the horrible-result shape. Entry 412 draws the neighbouring line: the slippery slope in its causal form claims that one step raises the chance of the next, a claim about the world, and the sorites shares only the machinery of vague predicates with it. The second error reads the borderline-contradiction result as people being illogical. What the data show is more orderly than that. Assent to 'tall and not tall' is highest at the middle case and near zero at the ends. Both contradictory forms sit below plainly true descriptions, and the gappy form beats the glutty one. The pattern tracks the structure of the stimulus rather than a failure of the law of non-contradiction. Alxatib and Pelletier's own account of it is pragmatic, that the conjunction is only interpretable on a weak reading of its parts. The third error is to expect people marched along a series to hang on to the first category. Introspection predicted that and the measurements went the other way in every ordered study read here: the switch comes earlier than random presentation gives, not later. Fourth, indiscriminability does not force co-categorisation. On Égré, Ripley and Verheyen's reading of the psychophysical work, two items too close to tell apart are highly likely to be named alike and not certain to be. That is what breaks the inductive premise, without anyone having to locate a sharp boundary. The colour experiments make the same point from the other side, since the order effect appeared in naming and not in perceptual matching. Last, the name. The fallacy lists carry this article under 'continuum fallacy', and none of the papers read here uses that phrase.

sources.text: Bonini, N., Osherson, D., Viale, R., & Williamson, T. (1999). On the Psychology of Vague Predicates. Mind & Language, 14(4), 377-393. Not obtained. The abstract and the bibliographic record were read at the Oxford University Research Archive. The design and the numbers attributed to it on this page were read in Alxatib and Pelletier's description of it.

Alxatib, S., & Pelletier, F. J. (2011). The Psychology of Vagueness: Borderline Cases and Contradictions. Mind & Language, 26(3), 287-326. The authors' manuscript was read in full as a PDF hosted on Paul Égré's seminar page; the Mind & Language version was not obtained. Every figure attributed to this study on this page was read in that manuscript, and the counts for the middling stimulus agree with the table Égré and Zehr reproduce from the published version.

Égré, P., de Gardelle, V., & Ripley, D. (2013). Vagueness and Order Effects in Color Categorization. Journal of Logic, Language and Information, 22(4), 391-420. Full text read from the manuscript on Égré's site. Source for the two colour experiments, the order effects and the hump effect.

Égré, P., & Zehr, J. (2018). Are Gaps Preferred to Gluts? A Closer Look at Borderline Contradictions. In The Semantics of Gradability, Vagueness, and Scale Structure, pp. 25-58. Springer. Full text read from the author copy deposited at HAL. Source for the 148-participant experiment, and for the figures quoted here from Ripley 2011 and from Serchuk, Hargreaves and Zach 2011.

Égré, P., Ripley, D., & Verheyen, S. (2019). The Sorites Paradox in Psychology. In S. Oms & E. Zardini (Eds.), The Sorites Paradox, pp. 263-286. Cambridge University Press. Full text read from the author copy at HAL. A review rather than a new experiment, and the source here for the two argument shapes, for the Fechner and Luce material on just noticeable differences, and for the descriptions of Hampton et al., Stöttinger et al., Raffman and McCloskey and Glucksberg.

Verheyen, S., Dewil, S., & Égré, P. (2018). Subjectivity in gradable adjectives: The case of tall and heavy. Mind & Language, 33(5), 460-479. Full text read from the author copy at HAL. Source for the correlations between a judge's own measurements and the threshold they use.

Serchuk, P., Hargreaves, I., & Zach, R. (2011). Vagueness, Logic and Use: Four Experimental Studies on Vagueness. Mind & Language, 26(5), 540-573. Not obtained; the publisher's copy is paywalled and the PhilPapers copy returned 403. The abstract was read at Crossref and on Zach's own site, and the counts quoted here come from the table Égré and Zehr build from this paper's data.

Ripley, D. (2011). Contradictions at the Borders. In Vagueness in Communication, Lecture Notes in Computer Science, pp. 169-188. Springer. Not obtained. Named here for the circle-and-square study, described on this page through Égré and Zehr's summary of its data.

Égré, P. (2015). Vagueness: Why Do We Believe in Tolerance? Journal of Philosophical Logic, 44(6), 663-679. Full text read from the manuscript on the author's site. Source for the general statement of the tolerance principle, for Wright's 1976 coinage, and for where each theory of vagueness stands on the principle.

Hampton, J. A., Estes, Z., & Simmons, C. L. (2005). Comparison and Contrast in Perceptual Categorization. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 31(6), 1459-1476. Not obtained. Named here for the contrast effect on borderline colour patches and the cat-to-dog morphs, as described by Égré, Ripley and Verheyen.

Stöttinger, E., Sepahvand, N. M., Danckert, J., & Anderson, B. (2016). Assessing perceptual change with an ambiguous figures task: Normative data for 40 standard picture sets. Behavior Research Methods, 48(1), 201-222. Not obtained. Named here for the 40 morphing picture sets and the rate of third-category naming, as described by Égré, Ripley and Verheyen.

McCloskey, M. E., & Glucksberg, S. (1978). Natural categories: Well defined or fuzzy sets? Memory & Cognition, 6(4), 462-472. Not obtained. Named here for the within-subject inconsistency in category membership judgements, as described by Égré, Ripley and Verheyen.
